You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 
on pages 6 and 7. 
Conserving plastic 
A 
In 1862 at the International Exhibition in London, a new material was first put on 
public display; the new material was plastic. Since that time many different forms of 
plastic have been developed and during the last century these plastics became an integral 
part of our lives. Many artefacts from the 20th century, from iconic items such as early 
Bakelite radios and iPods, to mundane goods such as children’s lunch boxes, are made 
from plastics. One of the most appealing aspects of plastics is their flexibility; they can 
be moulded into almost any shape imaginable, and are available in consistencies ranging 
from rock-hard to soft and malleable. 
 
B 
For much of the last century it was believed that these materials were indestructible. 
Since the late 1970s, however, as some of the items have become museum pieces, 
scientists and museum curators have found that the notion was sadly mistaken. When it 
comes to longevity, plastics have a serious weak spot. In molecular terms, plastics are 
chain-like carbon-based molecules that can be shaped when warm but become firm 
once cooled. Over time, the chemical bonds that hold these chains together are 
destroyed as they are attacked by oxygen in the air or by sunlight, or are simply broken 
apart by heat. The consequences of these processes are already being seen in materials 
and objects from the 19th and 20th centuries. Cinema film made from celluloid, for 
example, caused the movie industry to explode in more ways than one. Celluloid is in 
some respects an ideal medium for film, as it is both transparent and flexible, but it is 
also a close relative of another plastic, sometimes known as guncotton, which is an 
explosive. In hot weather celluloid became unstable and ignited spontaneously. As a 
result, many early Hollywood movies simply went up in smoke. 
 
C 
Other plastics decay in different ways. When the problems of using celluloid became 
understood, a non-flammable alternative was found. Unfortunately, this alternative, 
cellulose acetate, has its own inherent problems. Like many other plastics, when 
cellulose acetate starts to break down, it releases chemicals that attack its own molecular 
chains so that the plastic is in effect attacking itself, thus speeding up the rate of decay. 
One of these chemicals is acetic acid, the sour liquid that is the essential ingredient of 
vinegar. A Russian sculptor of the 1920s and 1930s, Naum Gabo, chose cellulose 
acetate as his sculpting medium. The Tate Modern gallery in London has a large 
collection of his works, many of which are from this period. In recent years, several 
have started to crumble without warning, giving off a distinct vinegary aroma as they do 
so. Without intervention, the same fate will eventually befall Gabo’s later sculptures, 
including one which sold for over £1 million at an auction in 2007. Although this

7 
 
sculpture was made from Perspex, a more durable plastic than cellulose acetate, it too 
will eventually decay back into basic molecular units. A similar fate awaits domestic and 
commercial doors, windows and water pipes which are of PVC (polyvinyl chloride). 
PVC often begins to decay after as little as a decade; the first sign of decay is when the 
surface becomes sticky and shiny. 
 
D 
These days the onset of decay in plastics can be put back significantly by adding anti-
ageing compounds that block the initial harmful effects of air and sunlight by acting like 
a sunscreen. Unfortunately, these additives are so costly that manufacturers do not use 
them unless absolutely necessary. Eventually, these additives also lose their 
effectiveness. Developing conservation strategies is made more challenging due to the 
variety of ways in which different plastics degrade. What works to preserve one material 
can catastrophically shorten the lifetime of another. Most modern plastics decay 
primarily through reactions with oxygen and are best preserved by sealing them in an 
oxygen-free atmosphere. Yet cellulose acetate needs exactly the opposite treatment: 
without a good supply of fresh air the decay is accelerated. 
 
E 
Conservation chemists from University College London have been working to find a 
way to be able to discover the type of plastic which plastic objects are made of. To this 
end they have developed a gun which shoots a wide spectrum of infrared light towards 
an object, and from this it is possible to build up a profile of the material from which 
the object is made. This is a non-destructive technique which the conservationists have 
already used to investigate the state of preservation of cultural artefacts which are not 
made of plastic, most notably the original notebooks of the scientist Charles Darwin, 
which record his thoughts and observations during his voyage on HMS Beagle and 
which formed the basis of his ground-breaking book on evolution: On the Origin of 
Species. 
 
F 
The infrared gun is being refined so that it will detect not only which plastic an object is 
made from, but also how degraded it has become. The task then is to devise methods of 
preserving objects, or at least inhibiting their decay. With limited knowledge and 
resources at their disposal, the conservationists have had to use a certain amount of 
improvisation. For example, one way is to freeze plastics to slow the process of decay, 
and another is to put them in airtight packaging often used by the food industry for 
meat. Lars Christensen of the National Museum of Denmark supports their work, 
believing that every generation of humans writes its own history through the artefacts it 
leaves to its successors. As our generation struggles to piece together the fragmentary 
records left behind by our ancestors, we should be mindful of our own legacy. He feels 
that if our plastic items were lost, it would very much affect how future generations 
would think of us.

Questions 20 and 21 
Choose TWO letters, A-E. 
Write the correct letters in boxes 20 and 21 on your answer sheet. 
The list below gives some of the reasons why the conservation of plastics is a difficult task. 
Which TWO of these reasons are mentioned by the writer of the text? 
 
A 
There are not enough trained conservationists. 
 
B 
Preservation have only a temporary effect. 
 
C 
New plastics are less stable than older ones. 
 
D 
Different plastics react differently to conservation techniques. 
 
E 
Museums are reluctant to spend money on conserving plastics.
